text: What is logistics?

options.text: Planning and controlling the movement and storage of goods
Selling products directly to final customers

why.B: Selling to final customers is a sales activity, not the overall logistics function.
why.C: Manufacturing creates products; logistics manages their movement and storage.
why.D: Vehicle repair is a maintenance activity, not the definition of logistics.

explanation: Logistics involves planning and managing how goods move and where they are stored. In trucking, it includes coordinating transportation so freight reaches its destination.
whyCorrect: Option A describes the movement and storage of goods, which are core parts of logistics.
basis: General trucking/logistics knowledge; this question tests a foundational term from the onboarding context.

text: Which company in the trucking process needs goods to be moved?

why.C: A driver operates the truck and moves the freight.
why.D: A loadboard is a platform where loads and available transportation may be posted.

explanation: A shipper is the person or business that has freight to send. The shipper typically needs a carrier to transport the goods to the destination.
whyCorrect: Option B identifies the party that sends or needs to transport the goods.

text: What is the main role of a freight broker?

why.A: Owning and operating trucks is associated with a carrier or owner-operator, not the broker’s defining role.
why.B: Trailer inspection and repair are maintenance functions.
why.D: Commercial driver’s licenses are issued by government licensing authorities, not freight brokers.

explanation: A freight broker arranges transportation by connecting a shipper that needs freight moved with a carrier that can move it. A broker generally does not perform the physical transportation itself.
whyCorrect: Option C captures the broker’s role as an intermediary between shippers and carriers.

text: Which statement describes a carrier?

options.text: A business that physically transports freight
A company that only stores inventory
A website used only to find fuel prices
A government agency that issues tax IDs

why.B: Storing inventory is a warehousing function.
why.C: A fuel-price website is a tool, not a transportation provider.
why.D: A government agency issuing tax IDs is not a carrier.

explanation: A carrier is a business that provides transportation for freight. In trucking, it arranges or performs the movement of goods using trucks and drivers.
whyCorrect: Option A describes the carrier’s transportation function.

text: Who is an owner-operator?

options.text: A driver who always uses a company-owned truck
An independent driver who owns and operates their truck
A broker who arranges freight without trucks
A shipper who sends products to customers

why.A: A driver using a company-owned truck is generally a company driver.
why.C: A broker arranges freight; that is a different role.
why.D: A shipper has goods to transport.

explanation: An owner-operator is an independent trucking business owner who owns and operates a truck, often working under a carrier’s authority or through business arrangements with carriers.
whyCorrect: Option B reflects the defining combination of ownership and operation of the truck.
basis: General trucking-industry knowledge; simplified for entry-level onboarding.

text: What is a key difference between a company driver and an owner-operator?

options.text: A company driver must own the truck
An owner-operator never pays operating costs
A company driver generally uses the company’s truck
An owner-operator cannot work with a carrier

why.A: Company drivers generally do not need to own the truck.
why.B: Owner-operators commonly have operating expenses such as fuel, maintenance, insurance, or payments on the truck.
why.D: Owner-operators can work with carriers under appropriate arrangements.

explanation: A company driver generally drives a truck provided by the employer or carrier. An owner-operator owns and operates their own truck and is typically responsible for business operating costs.
whyCorrect: Option C describes the usual distinction in truck ownership.

text: What does OTR mean in trucking?

why.A: This is not the meaning of OTR in the trucking context.
why.C: This is not the standard expansion used for this driver type.
why.D: This is not the standard trucking term.

explanation: OTR stands for Over-the-Road. It usually describes long-haul trucking that takes drivers over longer distances and often across multiple states.
whyCorrect: Option B is the standard expansion of OTR in trucking.

text: What does CPM mean when discussing driver pay?

why.A: Cost per month is not the meaning of CPM in this driver-pay context.
why.B: Cargo per mile is not the standard pay term.
why.D: Carrier payment method is not the standard expansion.

explanation: CPM means cents per mile when discussing driver pay. It indicates how many cents a driver earns for each mile driven under that pay arrangement.
whyCorrect: Option C is the pay-related meaning used in trucking.

text: What is the purpose of a trailer?

options.text: To hold cargo and be pulled by a tractor
To provide the engine power for the truck
To record a driver’s hours of service
To issue payment codes at a truck stop

why.B: The tractor, not the trailer, supplies the truck’s engine power.
why.C: Hours of service are recorded using required logs or electronic logging systems.
why.D: Payment codes are unrelated to a trailer’s function.

explanation: A trailer carries freight and is pulled by a powered truck tractor. The tractor provides the engine and driving power; the trailer is used to carry the load.
whyCorrect: Option A describes the trailer’s main purpose.

text: Which tractor cab is designed with a sleeping area for long-haul trips?

why.A: A day cab is generally designed for shorter trips where the driver returns without needing an onboard sleeping compartment.
why.C: Flatbed describes a trailer/load setup, not a standard cab type.
why.D: Reefer refers to refrigerated equipment, not a cab type.

explanation: A sleeper cab includes a sleeping compartment, making it suitable for drivers who spend nights on the road during long-haul trips.
whyCorrect: Option B names the cab type designed with a sleeping area.

text: What does CDL stand for?

why.B: Carrier dispatch log is not the expansion of CDL.
why.C: Cargo delivery label is not the expansion of CDL.
why.D: Commercial diesel limit is not the expansion of CDL.

explanation: CDL stands for Commercial Driver’s License. In the United States, drivers generally need the appropriate CDL class and endorsements for many commercial motor vehicles.
whyCorrect: Option A is the official term used for a commercial driving license.

text: What does DOT Medical Card confirm in the onboarding presentation?

options.text: The driver has passed a required medical examination
The driver has a fuel-card credit line
The driver has completed a freight delivery

why.A: Truck ownership is a separate matter and is not established by a medical card.
why.C: A medical card does not approve a fuel-card credit line.
why.D: A medical card is not a delivery record.

explanation: The DOT Medical Card is evidence that a commercial driver has met the applicable medical qualification requirements following a medical examination. It does not prove truck ownership or fuel-card approval.
whyCorrect: Option B describes the purpose of the medical qualification document.
basis: General U.S. trucking-industry knowledge; phrased to match the onboarding term.

text: What does IFTA relate to?

options.text: Fuel tax reporting for qualifying operations across states
The process of booking freight loads

why.B: Tire replacement is a maintenance matter, not IFTA.
why.C: Booking freight is a dispatch or brokerage activity, not IFTA.
why.D: Driver bonuses are unrelated to IFTA.

explanation: IFTA is the International Fuel Tax Agreement. It provides a system for qualified motor carriers to report and distribute fuel-use taxes across participating jurisdictions. The onboarding test uses this as a basic industry concept.
whyCorrect: Option A is the closest description of IFTA’s purpose.

text: What does HOS refer to?

why.B: Hauling Order System is not the standard term.
why.C: Highway operating speed is not the meaning of HOS.
why.D: Heavy operator standard is not the meaning of HOS.

explanation: HOS stands for Hours of Service. It refers to rules governing how long commercial drivers may drive and work before taking required breaks or rest periods.
whyCorrect: Option A is the standard expansion of HOS in trucking.

text: What is an ELD used for?

options.text: Finding the lowest fuel price at every station
Measuring the weight of a truck’s cargo
Issuing an MC number to a carrier

why.B: Fuel-price discovery is a separate function, such as a fuel finder tool.
why.C: Cargo weight is measured using weighing equipment or scales.
why.D: An ELD does not issue a carrier’s MC number.

explanation: ELD stands for Electronic Logging Device. In relevant commercial trucking operations, it electronically records driving time and helps support Hours of Service compliance.
whyCorrect: Option A describes the primary purpose tested here.

text: What does DEF stand for?

why.A: Diesel Efficiency Fuel is not the term’s expansion.
why.B: Driver Expense Form is not the term’s expansion.
why.D: Direct Engine Feed is not the term’s expansion.

explanation: DEF stands for Diesel Exhaust Fluid. It is used in the exhaust after-treatment systems of many modern diesel vehicles to help reduce certain emissions. It is not diesel fuel.
whyCorrect: Option C is the correct expansion of DEF.

text: When a driver says they are fueling a reefer, what are they usually fueling?

why.B: Washer fluid is unrelated to reefer fuel.
why.C: The air-brake system is not what a driver means by fueling a reefer.
why.D: A passenger cabin is not the refrigerated trailer unit.

explanation: In trucking, a reefer is a refrigerated trailer or its refrigeration unit. The unit commonly has a separate fuel tank and may use diesel to run the refrigeration equipment. The onboarding presentation specifically explains that “pumping reefer” refers to fueling this unit.
whyCorrect: Option A matches the explanation in the onboarding presentation.

text: According to the presentation, which fuel type receives the CFT discount?

why.B: The presentation does not state that gasoline receives the discount.
why.C: DEF is listed as a possible card use, but the presentation says the discount applies only to diesel.
why.D: Reefer is listed as a possible card use, but the presentation says the discount applies only to diesel.

explanation: The onboarding presentation explicitly states that the discount applies only to Diesel. Although the card may be used for other listed purchases or services, agents must not promise that the diesel discount also applies to DEF, reefer fuel, gasoline, or other items unless the company confirms separate terms.
whyCorrect: Option A follows the presentation’s note: “Discount ONLY applies for Diesel.”

text: Which statement about a freight broker is correct?

options.text: The broker must own the cargo
The broker connects the shipper and carrier and arranges transportation
The broker is always the truck driver’s employer
The broker maintains every truck in the fleet

why.A: The shipper typically owns or controls the freight; a broker does not have to own it.
why.C: The broker is not automatically the driver’s employer.
why.D: Truck maintenance is generally handled by the owner or operating company, not by every broker.

explanation: A freight broker typically arranges transportation between a shipper and a carrier. The broker does not necessarily own the freight, employ the driver, or maintain the carrier’s trucks.
whyCorrect: Option B describes the broker’s intermediary role.

text: What is one purpose of understanding competitors’ fees and network coverage?

options.text: To make unsupported claims about other cards
To compare offers accurately and explain relevant differences
To avoid learning the company’s own offer
To promise every customer the same savings

why.A: Unsupported claims can damage trust and mislead prospects.
why.C: Agents must understand CFT’s own offer as well as competitor offers.
why.D: Savings depend on usage and location; an agent should not promise the same result to every customer.

explanation: The onboarding presentation says agents should understand competitors’ fees, discounts, network coverage, and limitations so they can handle objections and explain CFT’s differences accurately. Comparisons should be fair and based on verified information.
whyCorrect: Option B reflects the presentation’s KYP (Know Your Product) guidance about competitor knowledge.
basis: Onboarding presentation, competitor analysis and KYP/KYC sections.

text: Which truck-stop brands are listed in the CFT offer?

options.text: TA, Petro, Love’s, Pilot, and Flying J
Walmart, Target, Costco, and Sam’s Club
Shell, BP, Exxon, and Chevron only

why.B: These are retail chains, not the truck-stop brands listed in the CFT offer.
why.C: These are delivery/logistics companies, not the listed truck-stop brands.
why.D: These brands are not the list provided in the CFT offer.

explanation: The CFT offer provided for this test names TA, Petro, Love’s, Pilot, and Flying J as participating truck-stop brands where cardholders are eligible for diesel discounts. Agents should use the approved current location tools to confirm specific locations and terms.
whyCorrect: Option A matches the brands named in the supplied offer.

text: What maximum diesel discount does the offer advertise compared with cash price?

why.A: This amount is lower than the maximum stated in the offer.
why.B: This amount is lower than the maximum stated in the offer.
why.C: This amount is lower than the maximum stated in the offer.

explanation: The supplied CFT offer states “Save up to $1.00 discount per gallon from cash price.” “Up to” describes a maximum advertised saving, not a guaranteed saving at every location or on every fill-up.
whyCorrect: Option D matches the maximum amount in the offer.
basis: User-provided CFT offer. Agents should avoid presenting the maximum as a guaranteed discount.

text: Which fee statement matches the CFT offer provided?

options.text: A monthly fee applies to every card
There are no transaction, swipe, deposit, monthly, or annual fees
A deposit is required for every truck
An annual fee applies after the first month

why.A: This contradicts the offer’s statement that there is no monthly fee.
why.C: This contradicts the offer’s statement that there is no deposit fee/requirement as described.
why.D: This contradicts the offer’s statement that there is no annual fee.

explanation: The supplied offer states there are no transaction, swipe, deposit, monthly, or annual fees. Agents should repeat these specific fee terms accurately and avoid adding claims about other possible charges that are not addressed in the offer.
whyCorrect: Option B reproduces the fee categories explicitly listed in the offer.

text: What weekly credit line does the offer state as the minimum per truck?

why.A: This is below the stated minimum.
why.B: This is below the stated minimum.
why.C: This amount is below the $5,000 minimum stated in the offer and appears in competitor material, not the supplied CFT offer.

explanation: The supplied offer says “Weekly credit line per truck minimum $5,000 within a payment twice weekly.” The test checks whether agents know the stated minimum. Agents should not describe it as an unconditional approval for every applicant unless company policy confirms eligibility and approval conditions.
whyCorrect: Option D matches the $5,000 minimum per truck stated in the offer.
basis: User-provided CFT offer; approval conditions are not specified in the supplied text.

text: According to the offer, how often are payments made for the weekly credit line?

why.A: Monthly payment frequency is not what the offer states.
why.B: Every two weeks is not the stated frequency.
why.D: Quarterly payment is not the stated frequency.

explanation: The supplied offer says the weekly credit line operates with payments twice weekly. Agents should communicate that stated frequency clearly. The exact payment days and mechanics are not specified in the offer supplied for this test.
whyCorrect: Option C matches “payment twice weekly.”
basis: User-provided CFT offer. Specific payment dates are not supplied.

text: How many discount locations does the CFT offer say are covered by the program?

why.A: This is below the number stated in the offer.
why.B: This is below the number stated in the offer.
why.D: This is above the number stated in the offer and is not supported by the supplied offer.

explanation: The supplied CFT offer states that more than 2,500 discount locations are covered by the program. Agents should use the company’s website or application to check current locations and applicable discounts rather than assuming every location offers the same discount.
whyCorrect: Option C matches the stated network size.

text: Which list matches the uses named in the CFT offer?

options.text: Diesel, DEF, truck scaling, reefer, and tire
Gasoline, groceries, hotels, tolls, and airfare
Diesel, car washes, restaurants, and entertainment
Gasoline, personal shopping, and household bills

why.B: These categories are not listed in the supplied CFT offer.
why.C: Car washes, restaurants, and entertainment are not listed in the supplied offer.
why.D: Personal shopping and household bills are not listed in the supplied offer.

explanation: The supplied offer lists Diesel, DEF, Truck scaling, Reefer, and Tire as available uses. Important distinction: the offer’s list of card uses is not the same as the diesel-discount rule. The onboarding presentation says the discount applies only to diesel.
whyCorrect: Option A matches the use categories listed in the offer.
basis: User-provided CFT offer; the diesel-only discount limitation comes from the onboarding presentation.

text: What customer-support availability is stated in the offer?

options.text: 12 hours a day, Monday to Friday

why.A: Weekday business hours are narrower than the advertised availability.
why.B: This is not the stated availability.
why.D: Weekend-only support is not the stated availability.

explanation: The supplied offer states 24/7 Customer Support, meaning support is advertised as available 24 hours a day, seven days a week. Agents should not promise a specific response time or resolution time unless the company has separately confirmed it.
whyCorrect: Option C matches the stated availability.

text: What does the offer say will be provided for an EFS money code?

options.text: A fixed $100 code for every customer
A code only for monthly payments
A code only after an annual fee is paid

why.A: The offer does not specify a fixed $100 amount.
why.C: The offer does not restrict the code to monthly payments.
why.D: The offer explicitly says there is no annual fee, and it does not state this condition.

explanation: The supplied offer says an EFS money code will be provided “for any amount.” The offer does not explain the process, limits, eligibility rules, or whether separate approval is required, so agents should not invent those details.
whyCorrect: Option B matches the wording in the supplied offer.
basis: User-provided CFT offer; process details are not supplied.

text: Which tools does the offer mention for monitoring and finding fuel-discount locations?

options.text: A paper map mailed each month

why.B: A mailed paper map is not mentioned in the offer.
why.C: A loadboard is not the tool described for checking fuel discounts.
why.D: A CDL portal is unrelated to monitoring CFT fuel discounts.

explanation: The supplied offer says customers receive access to a special website and application to monitor and check fuel-discount locations. Agents can describe these tools as a way to review locations, but should not claim features beyond what the company has confirmed.
whyCorrect: Option A matches the website and application named in the offer.
